title: Old Plastic Pipes Could Become Engine Oil
summary:
Old plumbing pipes, discarded window frames and expired credit cards could one day become valuable ingredients in engine oil.

Researchers at Virginia Tech have found a new chemical process that turns one of the world's hardest plastics to recycle into a high-performance lubricant material.

The team, led by chemist and chemical engineer Guoliang “Greg” Liu, turned polyvinyl chloride, known as PVC, into polyalphaolefin, a key ingredient in synthetic lubricants such as engine oil.

The research was published in the journal Nature. PVC is especially hard to recycle because it contains chlorine and a wide range of chemical additives.

Those additives give PVC different properties, such as flexibility, rigidity and resistance to heat, but they also complicate conventional recycling. As a result, much of the world's discarded PVC ends up in landfills.

Meanwhile, demand for lubricants keeps growing, and making them can come with significant environmental costs. Lubricants are essential to modern machinery: they reduce friction and wear between moving parts, helping engines run efficiently and last longer.

To make the new lubricant, the researchers place PVC like the kind used in household plumbing, window frames and credit cards into a solvent. They then add aluminum trichloride and alpha-olefins, a class of hydrocarbons used in making synthetic lubricants.

The mixture is heated to 158 degrees Fahrenheit for three hours, and then the researchers extract a relatively thick lubricating oil. The resulting polyalphaolefin belongs to a family of synthetic base oils valued for their stability, lubricating properties and ability to perform across a wide range of temperatures.

“Number one, we have proved that it is feasible to use plastic waste to make high-performance lubricants,” Liu said.

The work builds on earlier research from Liu's lab that turned other plastic waste into soap ingredients.
why_it_matters: Turning old plastic into useful oil could cut the amount of PVC buried in landfills and reduce the environmental cost of making new lubricants.
